title: Engines and humans 1: how machines took over chess
outcomes: Gives the dates and results of the 1996 and 1997 Deep Blue matches and the 2006 Bonn match, with a source for each
Says what the 1997 match shows and what it does not show (sample size, special hardware, a party to the match)
Reads a stepped game with a purpose for each move and separates a verified fact from a conjecture
Explains with a fortress position why a depth-limited engine score is not an outcome
Tests a source's claim against an engine and says what is unresolved

steps.caption: New York, May 1997, game 6. White to move. The knight on g5 can take the pawn on e6. Someone chose to do that: a person or a machine. Which? Decide before reading on.

steps.prompt: Human or machine, and why do you think so?

steps.text: **Answer: a machine, Deep Blue, with White.** Wikipedia calls the sacrifice a well-known refutation of the line Kasparov chose, so the idea was known human theory [S]. The same page says Kasparov expected a machine not to sacrifice without concrete gain [S]. So 'human or machine' was half a question: a machine played it, with a human idea behind it. We return to this with the engine's view.

steps.prompt: Were you right? What made you guess human or machine, and would you guess the same way now?

fields.label: my guess was right or wrong because:

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Tell the story of engines in dated steps, each with a source. Say what the Deep Blue games show and what they do not. Read a game with a reviewer's eye. Scores here come from one engine at depth 16 (it searched about 16 half-moves ahead) unless stated: evidence at that depth, not proof.

**Timeline [S].** February 1996, Philadelphia: Kasparov beat Deep Blue 4-2. May 1997, New York: Deep Blue won 3.5-2.5. IBM built the machine, so its history page is a party's account; Wikipedia's match article gives the same numbers. November to December 2006, Bonn: the program Deep Fritz beat Vladimir Kramnik 4-2 (Wikipedia). Sources are listed at the end.

steps.prompt: From memory: which match did the human win, and which did the machine win? Give city, month and score.

steps.text: **1996, game 1.** Deep Blue had White against Kasparov's Sicilian Defence, Alapin Variation, and won in 37 moves. Wikipedia calls it the first game a chess computer won against a reigning world champion at normal classical time controls [S]. Kasparov still won that match 4-2: one game won does not make a match.

**What was inside Deep Blue [S, I].** Wikipedia mentions an opening book, with an extended book built from a data set of 700,000 grandmaster games. That is stored human knowledge, not search. The rest, our reading [I]: the machine searched many moves ahead and scored each end position with an evaluation tuned by people. We did not read figures for its speed or hardware, so we give none.

steps.prompt: Deep Blue won game 1 in 1996 and still lost the match. What does that tell you about judging a machine, or a person, from one game? One sentence.

steps.text: **Game 1, 3 May 1997.** Kasparov had White and won in 45 moves [S, Wikipedia]. It began as a Reti-type opening that Wikipedia calls a King's Indian Attack. Watch what White does not do: no early central pawn break, both bishops aimed down long diagonals. The sentences describe what each move does, never what Kasparov was thinking. A board cannot tell us that.

steps.text: **Where did the sacrifice come from?** Wikipedia calls it a well-known refutation of Kasparov's set-up [S], so the idea was human theory before the match. Whether Deep Blue calculated it or had it stored in its opening book, we have no source [H]. Our engine ranks the sacrifice first, and prefers 7...Bd6 to Kasparov's 7...h6 [V]: the move order, not only the sacrifice, let it work [I].

steps.text: **What one match can and cannot show.** It shows that in May 1997 a machine built by a company, and prepared against this opponent, won a six-game match: three draws, one win for the human, two for the machine. It does not show that machines beat every human, or that the machine understood chess. Six games and one opponent are a small sample, the hardware was special, and IBM was a party to the match [S, I].

steps.prompt: Decide: 'The 1997 match proved computers play chess better than every human.' Is that supported, partly supported, or not supported, and what would you need to see?

steps.text: **A fair reading [H].** The 1997 loss mattered less for chess than for how people felt about computers. The match was a cultural turning point more than a technical proof. You may disagree: a match with fair terms could have been more convincing.

steps.prompt: Do you agree that the match was more a cultural turning point than a technical proof? Give one reason for and one against.

steps.text: **Software and open engines [S].** The 2006 Bonn match was won by Deep Fritz, a commercial program. Stockfish is an open-source engine. Its version 12, released on 2 September 2020, made NNUE (a neural-network evaluation) its default [Stockfish blog]. The project's own post says version 12 won far more game pairs than it lost against version 11.

**The neural era [S].** The paper Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play was first submitted to arXiv on 5 December 2017 (arXiv 1712.01815). Leela Chess Zero was announced on 9 January 2018 as an open project built on the same idea and adapted from the Go program Leela Zero; it won the engine championship TCEC season 15 in May 2019 (Wikipedia). We quote no AlphaZero match score: we read only the abstract page, and the score has one source.

steps.text: **Two ways to look.** An engine does two jobs: it searches (tries moves ahead) and it evaluates (judges the position it reaches). Early programs leaned on search speed. Neural evaluation lets a modern engine judge a position well after fewer lookups. [I] That is our reading of the sources above, not a measurement. The next two boards show what a search that is too shallow can miss.

steps.text: **Why the shallow score failed.** Depth 2 sees the pawn about to queen and counts it as won. The corner h8 is a dark square and this bishop is light, so it can never cover the corner: Black's king shuffles and stalemate follows. Depth 2 is far shallower than any 1997 machine, so this shows only that a shallow search misreads fortresses, nothing about Deep Blue [I]. Depth 16 gives about +0.7: better, yet not the true result, a draw. The contrast is score versus tablebase.

steps.text: **Using this.** When an engine score and your own sense disagree, ask what the score is blind to: a fortress, a stalemate, a position that needs a long plan. A score is a summary of a search; the board is the evidence. Later lessons use engines the other way round: engine last, after you have found the idea yourself.

**What a club player faces.** Deep Blue was a special IBM machine [S]. The engine in this app is Stockfish 19 lite, running in your browser [V]. How the two would score against each other we have not measured, so we make no claim [H]. What matters for you: a free engine is a tool in your hands, so the habits in this lesson (test the score, read the source) are yours to use.

steps.prompt: Name two differences between Deep Blue in 1997 and the engine on a phone today. One must be a dated fact from this lesson; one may be your own conjecture, marked as such.
Teach it back. Imagine a friend says: 'Computers solved chess in 1997.' Explain why that is not what happened.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you give a date and a source? Did you say what one match cannot show? Did you give an example a friend could set up on a board (the fortress works)? Did you mark one claim as your own guess? If you cannot answer one of these, reopen the matching board. The app grades none of this; you are the reviewer.

**Recap.** 1996: human won, 4-2. 1997: machine won, 3.5-2.5, under IBM's own organisation. 2006: Deep Fritz beat Kramnik. 2017 to 2020: neural ideas reached open engines. One match is a small sample. Scores are depth-limited evidence; fortresses and stalemates show why. Sources can disagree with an engine, and then you test, you do not pick a winner.

The move lists were replayed with python-chess: every move legal, final moves match the page (45.g7, 45.Ra6, 19.c4). Moves are facts; all comment on the moves is ours. Also read 2026-10-30 for this pass: the page calls 8.Nxe6 a well-known refutation and says Kasparov expected a machine not to sacrifice without concrete gain; the film Game Over (Greengard, Seirawan) on the end of game 2; 1996 game 1 (Sicilian, Alapin, 37 moves, first classical-time-control win by a computer over a reigning champion); the opening book and extended book of 700,000 grandmaster games. It gives no figures for Deep Blue's speed.
[S] Wikipedia, 'Deep Fritz', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Fritz, read 2026-10-30 (Bonn, 25 November to 5 December 2006; Deep Fritz won 4-2)

[S] Wikipedia, 'Leela Chess Zero', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leela_Chess_Zero, read 2026-10-30 (announced 9 January 2018; based on AlphaZero's idea; adapted from Leela Zero; TCEC season 15, May 2019). First 100000 characters read.

[S] Stockfish project blog, 'Stockfish 12', https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2020/stockfish-12/, read 2026-10-30 (released 2 September 2020; NNUE default; wins many more game pairs than it loses against version 11)

[S] IBM history page 'Deep Blue' and arXiv 1712.01815 abstract page (5 December 2017), as recorded in the earlier version of this lesson, accessed 2026-10-29; the AlphaZero match score is deliberately not used (single source)

[V] Engine claims: Stockfish 19 lite, single thread, depth 16 unless a claim states another depth; one-off depth 26 run for the game 2 resignation position (not re-run by the validator); tablebase claims from the Lichess 7-man service
[I]/[H] The cultural-turning-point idea, the search-or-preparation question, and the shallow search as a stand-in for old engines are conjecture, labelled as such in the text

[V] Engine recounts, 30 Oct 2026, Stockfish 19 lite single thread: game 2 position after 45.Ra6 about +0.9 to +1.1 for White at depths 16, 22 and 26 (runs differ slightly with hash size); 44.Kh1 first at depths 16 and 18, 1.1 to 1.9 pawns above 44.Kf1; 34...Qxf1+ 1.1 to 1.7 below 34...h5; fortress position, Black to move, about +0.7 at depth 16 and +9.6 at depth 2. The draw-rate comparison used in an earlier version was removed: it compared different populations.
